result:
The first thing I repaired at the Saturday repair café was a toaster. I say “repaired” because that is what I wrote on the form, but what I actually did was turn it upside down and shake it. A piece of toast fell out. The owner, a man named Leonard, watched me do this with the grave attention of someone observing a medical procedure he suspects he could have performed at home.

“How much?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

He looked at the toaster, then at me. “Well, you’ve priced it right.”

We worked in the basement of a library, beneath a room where children were learning to play the recorder. Every so often a note would come through the ceiling all by itself, as if one child had remembered something the others had forgotten. Our tables were marked ELECTRICAL, CLOTHING, BICYCLES, and OTHER. I sat at OTHER. In theory this was because I had a broad range of skills. In practice it was because I had arrived after everyone else had chosen a table.

The toaster was my only success for three weeks. I made a pepper grinder worse. I spent an hour trying to open a jewelry box before its owner mentioned that she had the key. When a woman brought in an umbrella that wouldn’t close, I got it closed, and we were both so pleased that neither of us thought to open it again until she was halfway up the stairs.

Then a girl named Nell brought me a globe.

It was the sort that sat in a cradle and spun on a tilted rod. The rod had snapped at the bottom, and the globe kept tipping out onto the table. Nell stopped it each time with the flat of her hand.

“Can you fix it without changing anything?” she asked.

“Probably,” I said, which was how I answered questions when I hadn’t yet looked at the thing.

She showed me what she meant. Someone had drawn a line across the globe in blue ballpoint pen. It started in Leeds, went diagonally down through the Atlantic, crossed the bottom of South America, and ended in open water. The line was faint in places where somebody had rubbed it with a thumb.

“My brother did that,” Nell said. “He thought if you went straight down from Leeds you’d come out in New Zealand.”

“He missed.”

“Yes, well, he was nine.”

She said this with the authority of someone who was now ten.

I took the globe out of its cradle and set it on a folded towel. At the top, the rod had a little brass cap that came off easily. At the bottom, the broken end was stuck inside a plastic fitting. I went to borrow a pair of pliers from the bicycle table.

When I came back, Nell had turned the globe so the blue line faced the ceiling.

“He says he didn’t do it now,” she said.

“Why?”

“He’s fourteen. He says that about most things.”

I pulled out the broken piece. It was shorter than I expected, which meant the rod had probably been loose for a long time. Under the table we kept a biscuit tin full of screws, washers, and pieces of things we had taken apart without ever getting them back together. Nell helped me spread the contents out. She was good at this. Most people looking for a small part move everything around at once. Nell picked up each piece, looked at it, and put it down somewhere she hadn’t looked yet.

We found a metal pin that was the right width but too long. I filed it down while she held the ruler. Upstairs, the recorders stopped. For a while the loudest thing in the room was a woman at the clothing table pulling a length of thread through a coat.

“What are you doing?” Leonard asked.

He had come back with the toaster. I thought, with a sinking feeling, that something else had gone wrong with it. Instead he set it down, plugged it in, and took a loaf of bread from his shopping bag.

“I’ve been thinking,” he said. “You should see it do one.”

It did two at a time. We ate standing up because every chair had something on it. Leonard had brought butter but no knife, so the woman from the clothing table washed her scissors and used the closed blades. Nell saved her crusts on a paper towel. She said she might want them later.

The pin fit. I put the globe back in its cradle and spun it harder than I meant to. We all watched it wobble. I reached to steady the base, but before I touched it, the wobble settled.

“Here,” I said.

Nell tried it herself, slowly. She stopped at the end of the blue line.

“What’s actually there?” she asked.

I leaned over. There wasn’t a name printed anywhere near it. The nearest lettering was so large that it seemed to describe half the world.

“Water, I think.”

“Just water?”

I was about to say yes. Then I remembered that when I was her age, I’d found a photograph of a man standing on the deck of a ship in weather so cold there was ice on the railings. I’d spent an afternoon trying to figure out which little patch of my school atlas he’d been standing in. I never found it. For months afterward, whenever I opened the atlas, I looked at the water first.

“I don’t know,” I said. “We could go upstairs and look.”

Nell considered this. From the stairwell her mother called that they were late. Nell tucked the globe against her chest. At the door she turned around, came back for the crusts, and put them in her coat pocket.

The next Saturday I found a library book on my chair. It was about the Southern Ocean. A slip of paper marked a photograph of a small gray bird riding a wave, its feet out of sight. On the slip, in handwriting I didn’t recognize, someone had written, *These sleep on the water.*

The book wasn’t checked out, so at closing time I took it upstairs. I meant to put it back on the shelf. Instead I got a library card.
